article_title: WebKit Says Safari and WebKit 27 Block Network Access to Identity Resolution Infrastructure, Targeting Email-Based Tracking

content_preview.title: WebKit Says Safari and WebKit 27 Block Network Access to Identity Resolution Infrastructure, Targeting Email-Based Tracking
content_preview.summary: In its iOS, iPadOS, macOS and visionOS 27 releases, WebKit blocks network access to identity resolution services at the domain level, so they cannot receive users' email addresses.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

The WebKit team has described a new tracking protection in its iOS, iPadOS, macOS and visionOS 27 releases. In a [WebKit blog post](https://webkit.org/blog/18438/blocking-identity-resolution-infrastructure/) dated October 19, 2026 and written by John Wilander, Charlie Wolfe and Matthew Finkel, the team states: "In our iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS 27 releases, Safari and WebKit block network access to identity resolution infrastructure to prevent cross-site tracking." editor_notes.content_quality: Briefing of 674 words (range 300-800) with Overview / What We Know / Context / What We Don't Know structure. Clear, scoped to what the post states.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read both snapshots from disk (source-0.html.gz = WebKit blog post 18438, HTTP 200, 41 KB; source-1.html.gz = webkit.org/tracking-prevention/, HTTP 200, 47 KB) and extracted raw text; also live-refetched the blog post via WebFetch (byline, date and lead sentence matched the snapshot). source-0 confirms: byline 'Oct 19, 2026 by John Wilander, Charlie Wolfe, and Matthew Finkel' (names exact, date exact); verbatim quotes all present: 'In our iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS 27 releases, Safari and WebKit block network access to identity resolution infrastructure to prevent cross-site tracking.'; 'invisibly collect your email address when you log in or sign up for a newsletter'; 'not themselves login providers or newsletter services'; 'all the downstream effects of that'; 'meaning they can't just change the structure of the network request to work around the protection'; 'almost always constitute Personally Identifiable Information, or PII'; 'First party personalization is not tracking, and is not what our technologies seek to prevent'; 'the central identity resolver is a third party'; 'fully blocked cross-site cookies six years ago'; the closing 'continue to prevent covert and cross-site tracking by default, while maintaining the ability for websites to provide first-party personalization to their users'. All quotes are attributed to the post/WebKit team/authors collectively, not to any single person. Platform list (iOS, iPadOS, macOS, visionOS) is exact; 'block network access' is described exactly as the post states it (domain-level blocking, so requests cannot be restructured to evade it); the article does not name blocked domains, does not claim other browsers follow, and does not claim more than the post. Identity resolution description (third-party collects email, opaque tracking ID permanently linked, ID stored on site, logout/unsubscribe does not remove it, identity graph, cross-device) matches. 'Targets email-based tracking' is supported: post says identity resolution is email-based and Hide My Email 'provide[s] additional protection against email-based tracking'. Hide My Email / iCloud+ description matches. source-1 confirms: default cookie policy 'to disallow a third-party to set new cookies unless it already has cookies' on Apple platforms and 'Third-party LocalStorage and IndexedDB are partitioned per first-party website'. source-1 does not mention identity resolution and the article does not claim it does. manifest suspicious_patterns null for both; no injection text found.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every number, name, date and quote traces to source-0 or source-1. Release status: the post says only '27 releases' and does not say whether Safari 27 is released or beta; the article does not assert a ship status or date, only 'releases', and its internal link to the Sep 25 Safari 27 article is consistent. The 'What We Don't Know' items (blocked providers and count; impact on legitimate login/newsletter flows; other engines' plans) are confirmed unstated in the post (live fetch also found no named domains/companies). The article states the post does not name domains and does not describe how the set is chosen; true.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral, attributive ('the post says', 'WebKit writes'). Claims about tracking harms are consistently attributed to WebKit rather than asserted in the Herald's voice. Apple/WebKit is a first-party source describing its own product; the article reports its own claims as claims and notes absent detail. Apple is in the same industry as competitors of Anthropic; no favourable or adverse framing was found, and sourcing is first-party only, which suits a product-behaviour announcement but offers no independent or industry-side view (acknowledged in unknowns).
editor_notes.originality: New topic; no existing article mentions identity resolution. Only related item is the Sep 25 Safari 27 article, which is linked as a prior report (developer-facing features) with no overlap.
concerns: Single-perspective sourcing (WebKit itself), which is inherent to the topic; no independent verification of which domains are blocked or of the post's claims about industry practice. Article attributes these claims properly.

Internal link /article/2026-09/25-safari-27-ships-with-... uses the correct singular form and resolves to src/content/articles/2026-09/25-safari-27-ships-with-safari-mcp-for-ai-coding-agents-customizable-select-styling-and-a-rewritten-ecmascript-module-loader.md.
recommendations: Follow up if WebKit or independent researchers publish the list of blocked domains or report breakage in login flows.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, well-attributed, neutral Briefing. No corrections needed. webkit.org is on config/source_allowlist.txt by exact hostname (line 844); no allowlist edit required.
